lesson.title: Hot, Cold, and Absolute: Comparing Temperature Scales
lesson.summary: Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin all measure the same physical quantity, the average kinetic energy of particles, but chemists rely on Kelvin because it starts at true zero motion rather than an arbitrary reference point.
lesson.body:
Temperature is a measurement, in the sense established in the Measurement unit, of how much average kinetic energy the particles in a sample of matter possess: the faster those particles move or vibrate on average, the higher the temperature. Three scales are used to report this quantity, and while they disagree on where zero falls and how big one degree is, they all describe exactly the same underlying physical reality, so any temperature can be converted from one scale to another without any loss of meaning.

The Celsius scale, used in most of the world and throughout chemistry for everyday work, sets 0 degrees at the freezing point of water and 100 degrees at the boiling point of water, both measured at standard atmospheric pressure, with the interval between them divided into 100 equal degrees. The Fahrenheit scale, still common in the United States for weather and cooking, sets water's freezing point at 32 degrees and its boiling point at 212 degrees, a span of 180 degrees, which is why Fahrenheit degrees are smaller than Celsius degrees. Converting between them uses the equations F = (9/5)C + 32 and C = (5/9)(F minus 32). For example, a comfortable room temperature of 22 degrees Celsius converts to F = (9/5)(22) + 32 = 39.6 + 32 = 71.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

The Kelvin scale is the one chemists actually prefer for calculations, because it is an absolute scale: 0 K, called absolute zero, represents the theoretical point where particles have the minimum possible kinetic energy, not simply the freezing point of some particular substance like water. Kelvin degrees, called kelvins and written without a degree symbol, are exactly the same size as Celsius degrees, which makes the conversion between them purely additive rather than requiring multiplication: K = C + 273.15. Water freezes at 273.15 K and boils at 373.15 K, the same 100 unit span as Celsius, just shifted up by 273.15.

Kelvin matters enormously in chemistry because many important equations, especially the gas laws you will encounter later, require an absolute temperature scale to work correctly. The relationship between gas volume and temperature, for instance, is directly proportional only when temperature is measured in kelvins, because that proportionality depends on temperature representing true particle energy starting from zero, not from an arbitrary point like water's freezing temperature. If you tried to use Celsius in a gas law calculation, a temperature of 0 degrees Celsius would incorrectly suggest the gas has zero volume or zero energy, which is physically wrong, since 0 degrees Celsius is actually 273.15 K, far above absolute zero.

As a worked example, suppose a chemistry problem gives a reaction temperature of negative 15 degrees Celsius and asks for the Kelvin value needed for a later calculation. Applying the conversion, K = C + 273.15 = negative 15 + 273.15 = 258.15 K. Because that number will typically be combined with other measured quantities, standard significant figure rules still apply when the final answer is reported, which is one more place where an earlier concept, Significant Figures, continues to matter even in a purely additive conversion like this one.
